title: Princess Tarakanova by Flavitsky: the flood, the rats and a legend that never happened
question: A woman in red, a flooding cell, rats climbing the bed. Who was she, and did she really die like this?

seo.meta_title: Princess Tarakanova: the Painting and the True Story
seo.meta_description: A guided look at Flavitsky's Princess Tarakanova (1864): the flooded cell, the rats, the woman who claimed to be an empress's daughter, and the legend.

intro: Princess Tarakanova is a painting by the Russian artist Konstantin Flavitsky, completed in 1864 and now in the State Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow. A young woman in a red dress stands on her bed in a prison cell of the Peter and Paul Fortress in Saint Petersburg, as floodwater pours through the barred window and wet rats climb towards her feet. The scene follows a famous legend. History tells a different story.

sections.heading: Who was she?
paragraphs: The woman known as Princess Tarakanova claimed to be the daughter of Empress Elizabeth of Russia. She even claimed to be a sister of the rebel leader Yemelyan Pugachev.
Empress Catherine II ordered her arrest. In May 1775 she was brought to the Peter and Paul Fortress and interrogated by Field Marshal Prince Golitsyn. She never revealed who she really was.

sections.heading: The legend and the record
paragraphs: The legend says she drowned in her cell during the great Saint Petersburg flood of 21 September 1777. That is the moment Flavitsky painted.

The records say otherwise. She died of tuberculosis on 4 December 1775, almost two years before the flood, and kept the secret of her birth even from a priest. The flood story stuck in popular memory largely because of this painting.

sections.heading: A painter's masterpiece
paragraphs: Flavitsky showed the painting at the Academy of Arts exhibition in 1864. It became his best-known work and helped earn him the title of professor of historical painting. The critic Vladimir Stasov called it "the glory of our school, the most brilliant creation of Russian painting".

Flavitsky died two years later, in 1866. Pavel Tretyakov acquired the painting for his collection after the artist's death. An earlier version from 1862 is in the Ekaterinburg Museum of Fine Arts, and a smaller 1864 version in the Penza Art Gallery.

meaning: Flavitsky painted a legend, not a fact, and he knew how to make it unforgettable: a beautiful young woman, a locked cell, water rising and no way out.
Seen today, the painting is also about how a powerful image can replace history. Most people who know the name Tarakanova know her from this picture, and from a death she never died.
whereToSee: State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow. Other versions are in the Ekaterinburg Museum of Fine Arts (1862) and the Penza Art Gallery.

details.headline: Saint Petersburg, 1777
details.text: A prison cell in the Peter and Paul Fortress. Outside, the river is flooding the city. Inside, a woman is trapped.

details.headline: The woman in red
details.text: She stands on her bed against the wall, head thrown back, eyes rolling up, as if she can no longer bear to look.

details.headline: A dress for a palace
details.text: A red velvet gown over white silk, lace at the sleeves: the dress of a woman who claimed royal blood, now in a cell.

details.headline: The barred window
details.text: High on the right, the only window is barred. Through it, the light of the flooded city.

details.headline: The water comes in
details.text: Water pours through the window and spreads across the floor. There is nowhere left to stand except the bed.

details.headline: Rats
details.text: Look at the pillow: a wet rat has climbed out of the water, crawling towards her.

details.headline: A prison meal
details.text: On the little table: a jug and a piece of bread. All she was given.

details.headline: The flood
details.text: Below, the floor is already under water, rising around the legs of the bed.

details.headline: But it never happened
details.text: The records say she died of tuberculosis in December 1775, two years before the flood. Flavitsky painted the legend, and the legend won. Who do you think she was?
